Illum oportet crescere, istum autem minui.
One must increase; the other must decrease.
The magnus homo, the great man, “reaches up toward divinity.” He becomes a manufacturer.
The parvus homo, the little man, becomes “more animal than an animal.” He becomes a manufactured product.
The wolf is really still a very human category.
Compared with the manufactured products of the brave new world, the wolf is still a creature.
The true intensifications, in the direction of both good and evil, arise only with the intervention of spirit.
The most astonishing document of the abyssal depth of German Idealism:

“But if spiritual contingency, arbitrary will, goes so far as evil, even this is infinitely higher than all of nature—higher than the lawful course of the stars or the innocence of the plant—for that which goes astray in this way is still spirit.”
The most evil, lowest wickedness of the human spirit is still greater than the starry heavens and the most beautiful flower. Because what goes astray in this way is still spirit.
What a sentence for our German situation in 1944!
The generation immediately after Hegel gave its answer:

Truly, the new products created by the breakdown of this philosophy will be stronger than every attempt to restore the old Churches. They will unleash theurgic forces—forces that try to make divine powers real in the world—that will make our miserable self-righteous people on both right and left shudder, along with all those who profit from the gigantic humiliation of the German people.

Instead of the renouveau catholique, the Catholic revival that took place between 1910 and 1933 and went unnoticed by official institutions, we shall now experience a fantastic retour offensif: a counterattack by the philosophy of German Idealism, armed with myth—which in reality means armed with theurgy.
Hegel above all. He will cease to be, in theory, a museum piece preserved by academic philosophy, and in practice, a weapon monopolized by Moscow Marxism.

If Heidegger, with his acts of re-ontologizing, can produce such broad effects even in Gallia docens, teaching and learned France, what depth of effect will Konrad Weiss’s “Christian Epimetheus” have in Germany!
Werner Blischke was supposed to discover the identity of the I. K. who wrote an article on Sartre in issue no. 4 of Kurier, 6 January 1948:
The idea was to verify the immanent existentialism of the article. But the author could not be identified.
“It is a human plan to interrupt history, in order to leap out of history and arrive at a stable perfection.”
That is illuminating for understanding Marx.
Marx’s claim to be “scientific” means claiming that one can change the world without leaping out of history.
The machine is the instrument assigned to utopia. It is the weapon used to carry out the plan.
The machine differs from the tool because, within itself, it transcends the human being who operates the tool—the craftsman.
Utopia is already present in this transcendence.

The machine dethrones the human being. It removes him from his place. That is the deeper meaning of Adolf Caspary’s The Machine Utopia (1930), which attacks the illusion that the machine could solve the problem created by the masses.
For Marx, the machine is the means of changing the world without leaping out of history.
What does the destruction of the island of Heligoland in 1947/48 mean?
A piece of land is turned into sea. It is sunk into the sea.
Its population is evacuated as refugees. For the first time in history.
U-topia: the transformation of a place with an exceptionally strong sense of location into nothing.
The nervousness of a hunted animal when a shot is fired.
The objective powers that only yesterday seemed so interesting to me, so worthy of legal and theoretical construction, now reveal themselves as heartless enemies.
A constant shift between the subjective and the objective.
The heralds of subjectivity deceive one another, whether the name is Max Stirner or James Joyce. But objective greatness already means, in itself: a poor, deceived, plundered subject.
A political complex of power is much more objective. But ultimately even that is nothing more than an état d’âme, a state of the soul.
A Hero’s Life in the style of Richard Strauss—with the hero’s companion perhaps thrown in as a finale in the style of Brother Straubinger—all of that has become foolish, cloudy foam.
Better, perhaps, the happiness of the gnat in the style of Rossini.
The animals of the forest and the flowers of the field.
Life and creation arising directly from matter itself.
The blissfully accelerated circulation of the blood.
The removal of the barrier of nature so that we can have direct, unrestricted access to natural nature.
To abolish all distance, and therefore every perspective.
Not even the giving of form: the unfolding of form.
All of these still imply distance, perspective, difficulty, a falling-away from the pure immanence of the immediate, natural, unobstructed here-and-now and of bodily existence without problems.
Do you see now which side the logic of pure democracy lies on? And who will find the absolution of the World Spirit for every atrocity, even the most inhuman ones?
Now we Germans are everything at once.

We are the περισσόν, as the Pythagoreans called it: the excess that goes beyond equilibrium, disturbing and yet fertile. We are περισσόν and περίψημα—the excess and the refuse, the cast-off thing. And at the same time we are the ἄτοπον: the thing that has no proper place.
The point and moment when one opposite passes into the other, while itself being neither one.
The point of μεταβολή, of transformation.
The ἐναντίον, the opposite that participates in what is different from itself and yet remains independent.
The moment in which things are neither separated nor mixed—οὔτε διακρίνεται οὔτε συγκρίνεται—as Plato’s Parmenides puts it.
I am the ἄτοπον against utopia!!
The space I gain is the ἄτοπον!!
From the intellectual side, I admired the cleanliness and precision.
From the moral side, I admired the patience and self-control with which you erected a systematically thought-out structure of legal argument while fully aware that beneath it opened a gaping abyss.
The gaping abyss is, of course, the unanswered question: whose authority are German courts and administrative authorities actually exercising today?
The concept of subjugation, which you deliberately avoid bringing to the foreground, serves as the legal vehicle for an intermediate condition.

The fundamental injustice of this condition seems to me to lie in the fact that the eternal connection between protection and obedience—a connection valid even in Hobbes’s state of nature—has been torn apart.
The person who has been subjugated obeys, and despite obeying is cast into misery.

Let me tell you at once, with surrealist openness, that the word—and still more the concept—Gesetz, “law,” fills me with horror and dread in every possible way: conceptually; intellectually; through psychological association; and, last but not least, even through its sound.
What horrifies me are the orgies of Setzen—of setting, positing, laying down—and the terror of the “positing of posits” into which we have been drawn since 1848 as though into the Maelstrom.
I am prepared to spend hours giving you examples and evidence: historical; linguistic and etymological; conceptual and systematic; constitutional; and from natural law.
Everything that is positively posited and posed is now struck by this curse.
Just as every “will to” anything whatsoever is now intellectually exhausted and condemned by history. And yet the positivist Walpurgis Night will continue to intensify for some time.
We shall have to drink the foul brew down to the dregs. So I suppress my horror and ask instead: do you think it is possible to repair the bankruptcy of the legislator by beginning from the judge?
